titleStmt.title: Schedulability Analysis and Priority Assignment for Segmented Self-Suspending Tasks

analytic.title: Schedulability Analysis and Priority Assignment for Segmented Self-Suspending Tasks

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Self-suspending behavior in real-time embedded systems can have a major and non-trivial negative impact on timing predictability. In this work, we investigate how to analyze the schedulability of segmented self-suspending task systems under a fixed-priority assignment. For this purpose, we introduce the multi-segment workload function as well as the maximum workload function in order to quantify the maximum interference from the higher-priority tasks when constructing our (sufficient) schedulability test. Moreover, we derive an optimal priority assignment with respect to our schedulability test since it is compatible with Audsley's Optimal Priority Assignment (OPA). We show by means of comprehensive evaluations that our approach is highly effective concerning the number of schedulable task sets. Furthermore, one set of results reveals a rather non-intuitive observation, namely, that the worst-case suspension time of a computation segment should also be respected to improve the schedulability even if the suspension may finish earlier.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In the field of real-time and embedded systems, it is a common case that tasks are suspended during resource access. Such situations may, for instance, occur when an I/O operation involving external devices is performed or when tasks are synchronized [14], [29]. The duration of these so-called selfsuspensions can range within an interval from a few microseconds (e.g., a write operation on a flash drive [16]) to a few hundred milliseconds (e.g., computation offloading to GPUs [17] and indeed has a major impact on timing predictability in terms of hard real-time schedulability analysis [28]. Especially within the scope of embedded cyber-physical systems, selfsuspensions take place quite frequently, engendered by interactions with the system's physical environment like, e.g., data measurement via sensor hardware.

The problem of scheduling real-time systems with selfsuspensions has been proven to be N P-hard in the strong sense, i.e., pertaining to uniprocessor setups, no polynomialtime algorithm for this problem does exist unless P = N P [28]. However, a number of approaches have been developed by the research community in order to formally express systems of this kind, such as the dynamic self-suspension task model, the segmented (or multi-segment) self-suspension task model as well as hybrid models (further information about this topic is provided in the survey by Chen et al. [10]).

Considering the dynamic self-suspension task model (cf. [9], [15], [22]), a task τ i is characterized by a quadruple (C i , S i , T i , D i ), where C i denotes each task instance's worstcase execution time, S i its worst-case suspension time, T i the minimum inter-arrival time between two jobs (also known as period), and D i the relative deadline. A task is permitted to suspend itself at any point in time, provided that the upper bound on suspension time is not overshot. This concept is preferably adopted if detailed knowledge such as the length and number of computation segments as well as of suspension intervals is not available at design time. Hence, the dynamic self-suspension model offers a reasonable opportunity to depict systems exhibiting self-suspending behavior despite a certain information uncertainty, but, as a consequence, suffers from pessimistic schedulability (for details refer to [30]).

Provided that more detailed information about the actual self-suspension pattern of a task is given in advance, it is possible to describe the respective task by means of the more precise segmented self-suspension task model. Here, a selfsuspending task is supposed to consist of M i computation segments alternating with M i -1 suspension intervals, represented as an array (C 1 i , S 1 i , C 2 i , S 2 i , ..., S Mi-1 i , C Mi i ), where each suspension takes place for at most S j i time units and hence the task's total execution time is upper bounded by C i = Mi j=1 C j i and the total suspension time by S i = Mi-1 j=1 S j i , respectively. However, although this paradigm enables us to compute tighter bounds on a task's worst-case response time, it entails a certain loss of flexibility.

In order to attain both precision and flexibility, a hybrid model for self-suspending real-time tasks has been recently proposed by von der Brüggen et al. [30], harnessing pre-known information about possible execution paths of a task in order to reduce pessimism in the analysis.

div.head: A. Related Work
div.p: In the past years, several new results have been obtained with respect to the analysis of task systems with selfsuspension. Unfortunately, many of these have been flawed and thus are omitted at this point. Besides, since this work focuses on the segmented self-suspension model under fixedpriority preemptive scheduling, only related publications are discussed here. A comprehensive survey addressing the flawed concepts and results can be found in [9], a survey of the current state-of-the-art in [10].

In 2016, two independent results from Chen [7] and Mohaqeqi et al. [24] showed that testing the schedulability of segmented self-suspending real-time tasks under fixed-priority scheduling is N P-hard in the strong sense. In 1998, Palencia and Harbour [27] modeled the gap between the best-case response time and the worst-case response time of a higherpriority computation segment as the release jitter of the computation segment. This is called dynamic offset in [27]. In 2015, Nelissen et al. [25] published a mixed integer linear programming (MILP) formulation suitable for the worst-case response time computation of self-suspending tasks, which has been shown to be flawed and was corrected and revised in 2017 [26]. However, the major disadvantage of the proposed method is the fact that with growing problem complexity, the time complexity becomes exponential. Moreover, the actual self-suspension property of a higher-priority task is abandoned during the analysis, since each task with self-suspending behavior is transformed into a set of common sporadic tasks. Apart from this, the matter of assigning task priorities has not been addressed in their work. In addition to the result regarding computational complexity by Mohaqeqi et al. [24], they proposed an abstraction refinement technique to test the schedulability when the higher-priority tasks are ordinary sporadic real-time tasks and the lowest-priority task is a segmented self-suspending task. They did not discuss any extension to cover cases where all tasks may suspend. Huang and Chen [13] presented a fixed-priority fixed-relative-deadline (FRD) approach with a bounded speedup factor under the well-known deadline-monotonic scheduling by extending the FRD approach by Chen and Liu [8] under dynamic-priority scheduling.

Unlike the aforementioned work, Kim et al. [19] do not omit the issue of priority assignment, but, instead of a tasklevel priority assignment, equip each individual computation segment with a particular priority (a pessimistic schedulability test was provided in an erratum [18] later).

div.head: B. Contributions
div.p: In this work, we propose a pseudo-polynomial time schedulability test for segmented self-suspending task systems under a fixed-priority assignment and prove that it is compatible with Audsley's Optimal Priority Assignment algorithm [1]. Our contributions are as follows:

• We derive the multi-segment workload function and, resulting from this, the maximum workload function to safely bound the interference a segmented selfsuspending task suffers from higher-priority tasks in Sec. III. • We provide a sufficient pseudo-polynomial time schedulability test for fixed-priority segmented self-suspending task systems in Sec. IV. • We prove that the proposed schedulability test is OPA compatible in Sec. V. • In Sec. VI, we show by comprehensive evaluations that our approach is competitive with the state-of-theart method for segmented self-suspension task systems and performs better than the state-of-the-art regarding dynamic self-suspension systems under most settings.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: Consider a uniprocessor system executing a set of n sporadic, independent, preemptive, segmented self-suspending real-time tasks τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n }. Each task τ i releases an infinite number of task instances, called jobs, and is characterized by a tuple
div.formula: (C 1 i , S 1 i , C 2 i , S 2 i , . . . , S Mi-1 i , C Mi i ), T i , D i
div.p: , where C j i qualifies the j th computation segment's worst-case execution time, S j i the actual (maximum) suspension time of the j th suspension interval, T i the minimum inter-arrival time between two task instances, and D i the task's relative deadline. The deadlines are assumed to be constrained, i.e., D i ≤ T i for all τ i . In addition, a job's response time is defined as the completion time of the last computation segment subtracted by the job's release time. Hence, the worst-case response time R i of task τ i is defined as the maximum response time amongst all its jobs. The utilization of task τ i is defined as
div.formula: U i = C i /T i .
div.p: De facto, the duration of the j-th suspension interval of a task τ i can be situated within the interval [ Sj i , Ŝj i ], where Sj i specifies the lower bound and Ŝj i indicates the upper bound on the particular time value. Hence, the minimum and maximum total suspension time per task can be expressed as

If a task does not suspend itself, it can be described as a common sporadic task, i.e., τ i = (C i , T i , D i ), and be directly included into our analysis. Besides, it may be the case that a task instance begins or completes its execution with a suspension interval. This can be handled by reducing the relative deadline of the task by the maximum length of the respective suspension interval.

We focus on task-level fixed-priority scheduling, i.e., each task is endowed with an immutable priority, so that all jobs released by the same task are scheduled on the same priority level and the system executes the highest-priority job located in the ready-queue at any point in time. If a job suspends itself, it is removed from the ready-queue until it returns from suspension. The priority assignment of a task set τ is a bijective function π : τ i → {1, 2, . . . , n} whereat 1 indicates the highest and n the lowest priority level. For each task τ k the set of tasks with higher priority than τ k is denoted by hp(τ k ).
We presume that C i + Ŝi ≤ D i for each τ i ∈ τ and n i=1 U i ≤ 1 since otherwise the task set is not schedulable by any scheduling algorithm by default.

div.head: III. WORKLOAD ANALYSIS
div.p: Aiming to generate a feasible schedule, it is necessary to determine all tasks' worst-case response times R i . However, this process requires precise information about the interference a task τ i suffers from higher-priority tasks. Although several workload functions have been developed for the analysis of dynamic self-suspension systems (cf. [15], [22]), applying these is not recommendable since additional information provided by the segmented self-suspension model is neglected in this case and, as a consequence, the analysis becomes unnecessarily pessimistic. Concerning the segmented selfsuspension model, workload functions have been proposed for task systems being scheduled according to a dynamic priority policy, namely, under a fixed relative deadline approach (cf. [8], [31]). For a similar scheduling strategy, workload functions are known as well considering the hybrid selfsuspension model [30]. However, these are not applicable in the contemplated case owing to the disparate scheduling concepts. In fact, workload-functions have also been proposed regarding segmented self-suspending tasks under fixed-priority scheduling (cf. [6], [20]), but, alas, the respective approaches have been proven to be flawed (with respect to [20], refer to [25], for [6], to [5]). Against this backdrop, we intend to derive a novel and tight workload function for segmented selfsuspension systems subsequently. Unlike in terms of non-suspending sporadic tasks, the critical instant theorem [23], i.e., each task's response time becomes maximal when all tasks are released simultaneously and their particular jobs become ready for execution as early as possible, cannot be employed to identify higher-priority tasks' interference and thus to compute a task's worst-case response time in the self-suspending case. The fact that releasing all tasks synchronously does not necessarily lead to the maximum interference a self-suspending task may suffer but that the critical instant rather depends on the timing characteristics of a task can be illustrated by the following example: Consider a self-suspending task τ 1 = ((1, 1, 2), 8, 8) scheduled along with a lower-priority non-suspending sporadic task τ 2 with period T 2 ≥ 8 and relative deadline D 2 ≥ 8. As pictured in Fig. 1, for C 2 = 1.5 execution time units, a critical instant occurs when τ 2 is released concurrently to the first computation segment of τ 1 . If, in contrast, C 2 = 0.5 execution time units, a critical instant can be caused by τ 2 being activated concomitantly to the second computation segment of τ 1 .

The lack of an established critical instant theorem discussed above is also observed in [7], [24], [25]. In light of this, it is apparent that we are committed to quantify the interference from higher-priority jobs in a different way. More precisely, the so-called carry-in job must be taken into account, i.e., a job of task τ k being released before the respective job of a contemplated task τ i but interfering with its execution. For clarification, consider two tasks τ 1 and τ 2 with τ 1 having higher priority than τ 2 , as given in Fig. 2. The second job of τ 1 is released strictly previous to the second job of τ 2 but suspends itself for an amount of time that is sufficiently large to interfere completely with τ 2 and thus to delay its execution.

However, in order to compute an upper bound on the worstcase execution time of a task τ i in a given interval of time [t 0 , t 0 + t], it is not sufficient to take only the carry-in job into account. Instead, it is necessary to also pay closer attention to each body job, i.e., a job of τ i being released and having its absolute deadline in the interval [t 0 , t 0 + t), as well as to the tail job, i.e., the last job of τ i released (but not necessarily finished) within the respective interval. The carry-in, body, and tail job of a task τ i are indicated in Fig. 3c.

div.head: B. Maximum Workload Function
div.p: Instead of enumerating all possible combinations of the sequences, we take an approximation to reduce the time complexity of the resulting schedulability test as follows: Definition 2. For a self-suspending sporadic task τ i , the maximum workload in an interval of length t is given by:
div.formula: Wi(t) = max h i ∈{1,...,M i } {W h i i (t)}(7)
div.p: Hence, for a task τ k and a given interval length t, an upper bound on the overall interference from all higher-priority tasks can be obtained by:
div.formula: W k (t) = k-1 i=1 Wi(t)(8)
div.p: Please note that this technique leads to a certain level of pessimism, as explained at the end of Sec. III-A.

div.head: IV. RESPONSE TIME ANALYSIS
div.p: Having introduced a method to safely bound the interference of higher-priority tasks on a self-suspending sporadic task τ k , we henceforth investigate how to analyze the response time of task τ k . The respective analysis process as a matter of fact bears some pitfalls that must be avoided carefully.

Naively, one may release task τ k along with all interfering higher-priority tasks and simply calculate its response time employing the maximum workload function based on the resulting schedule. This approach, however, may generate an overoptimistic worst-case response time value depending on the actual moment of the contemplated task's activation. By way of illustration, consider two self-suspending sporadic tasks τ 1 = ((0.5, 3, 0.5), 4, 4) and τ 2 = ((6, 2, 1), T, T ) with Ti -Di τ i t 0 + t t 0 f σi (a) An example schedule where f σ i < t 0 . In the first case, portrayed in Fig. 6a, τ 2 is released synchronously with the second computation segment of τ 1 , so that, in consequence, a response time of 11 execution time units is attained. Fig. 6b, in contrast, shows a distinct case where τ 2 is released asynchronously to τ 1 and thus exhibits a response time of 12 execution time units.

In avoidance of such erroneous assessments, it is crucial to specify an upper bound on the analyzed task's response-time. To fulfill this objective, two distinct modeling techniques can be applied, namely, the Suspension as Computation (SC) as well as the As Interference Restarts (AIR) paradigm, which shall be examined more in detail hereinafter.

Employing the SC method, also known as suspensionoblivious approach [9] or joint [4], each suspension interval of τ k is modeled as a computation segment of Ŝj k , i.e., τ k is assumed to continue executing during its suspension intervals. Resulting from this, the aggregate of its computation segments and suspension intervals can be treated as a regular, nonsuspending sporadic task with regard to response time analysis and thus to calculate an upper bound on the response time of task τ k . This is summarized by the following theorem: Theorem 2 (SC). Therefore, the worst-case response time R k with R k ≤ T k equals the minimum t satisfying

div.p: In order to test the schedulability of a task set, the worstcase response time of each task has to be computed by Theorem 2 successively, beginning with the highest-priority task in the system. In each iteration of testing τ k , τ k is identified as schedulable if R k ≤ D k , while it is deemed unschedulable if Theorem 2 cannot be applied. More precisely, this is the case if R k > T k , since Theorem 2 is only suitable for computing the worst-case response time of task τ k if R k ≤ T k . The task set is determined to be schedulable if Theorem 2 holds for each of the tasks τ k above.

Unfortunately, on some occasions, the response time upper bound R * k resulting from Theorem 2 may become overly pessimistic when applying the SC technique to segmented selfsuspending tasks. This is often the case in scenarios where either the ratio Ŝk C k becomes large or the suspension intervals of τ k are longer than the periods of some interfering tasks. Two related examples are given subsequently. Consider an example provided in [9]: A segmented selfsuspending task τ 3 = ((1, 5, 1), 15,15) is transformed to a task τ 3 = (7, 15, 15) by means of SC, which is scheduled along with two non-suspending, higher-priority sporadic tasks τ 1 = (2, 5, 5) and τ 2 = (2, 10, 10). The resulting task set is not schedulable, since the total utilization of τ 1 , τ 2 , and τ 3 is greater than 1, although a task set consisting of τ 1 , τ 2 , and τ 3 is indeed schedulable (for details refer to [9]).

More precisely, for τ 2 to be schedulable on an α-speed processor when τ 2 and the second computation segment of τ 1 are released simultaneously, it must hold that

Hence, α → ∞ when T F → ∞. In order to overcome the potential pessimism introduced by the SC method, the concept of AIR (as interference restarts) can be adopted, availing the underlying idea to individually compute the response time of each single computation segment that suffers maximum interference from higher-priority tasks, as explained in what follows: Lemma 3. The worst-case response time of a computation segment C j k is upper bounded by the smallest value R j k ≤ T k satisfying

div.p: where W i (R j k ) is defined in Def. 2. Proof. The above statement can be proven by contradiction. Assume that a computation segment C k j is released at time t 0 and has the response time R j k > R j k . Due to the selfsuspending sporadic task model as well as the assumption that each task's worst-case response time does not overshoot its period, it is evident that at t 0 no other computation segment of task τ k is ready for execution except C j k . Since, according to our assumption, the response time R j k of C j k is greater than R j k , C j k cannot be finished within the busy interval [t 0 , t 0 +R j k ]. In compliance with Theorem 1 and Def. 2, the accumulated execution of each task is upper bounded by W i (t) for a given interval length t. Owing to the fact that t 0 + R j k is the point in time at which R j k = C j k + τi∈hp(τ k ) W i (t), the execution of segment C j k must be completed at time t 0 + R j k , exhibiting a response time of no more than R j k , which is a contradiction to the assumption.

Building on this, an upper bound on the worst-case response time of τ k can be obtained by summing up all computation segments' individual upper bounded worst-case response times as well as the total suspension length. Thus, the subsequent Theorem directly follows from Lemma 3: Theorem 3 (AIR). The worst-case response time of a task τ k is upper bounded by

div.p: where R j k ≤ T k is the smallest value satisfying Lemma 3. Heretofore, we introduced two distinct approaches to determine an upper bound on a self-suspending sporadic task's worst-case response time, but, however, to ensure an estimation that lacks unnecessary pessimism, the proposed concepts can be combined to a pseudo-polynomial time method: Theorem 4 (SCAIR). A sporadic self-suspending task τ k is schedulable under a fixed-priority policy if, according to the lowest bound obtained by either SC (applying Theorem 2) or by AIR (availing Theorem 3), task τ k meets its deadline, i.e., R * k ≤ D k , for a given priority assignment. Proof. This follows directly from Theorems 2 and 3.

The pseudo-polynomial runtime complexity emerges from the fact that the conditions in Theorem 2 and Lemma 3 can be checked in polynomial time. Hence, the complexity results from the number of points in time that need to be tested to determine the values of R * k and R j k . Analogously to the wellknown Time Demand Analysis (TDA) [21], (in the worst-case) it is sufficient to consider all points in time where the workload function begins to change. This coincides with the moment a computation segment is released in one of the alignments. Since for each task τ i , M i alignments exist and, moreover, in each alignment M i segments are released, A given task τ i can be released at no more than M 2 i points in time. It is also known from TDA that the maximum number of jobs released in one period of τ k is pseudo-polynomial. For τ k , such an analysis is performed M k + 1 times. Therefore, the resulting time-complexity is pseudo-polynomial.

div.head: V. PRIORITY ASSIGNMENT
div.p: Up to now, we derived a workload function for the segmented self-suspension task model and applied it in order to determine an upper bound on a task's worst-case response time. As a next step, the topic of finding a reasonable fixedpriority assignment shall be addressed aiming to feasibly schedule the contemplated task set.

Concerning non-suspending sporadic real-time tasks with constrained deadlines, deadline-monotonic scheduling is commonly known to be an optimal fixed-priority policy. However, regarding implicit-deadline task sets with self-suspension, it has been shown that no lower bound on the speed-up factor can be guaranteed for rate-monotonic scheduling [8] (the suboptimality of deadline-monotonic scheduling for constrained deadline task sets follows directly). Hence, it is advisable to find another solution. At this juncture, the so-called Optimal Priority Assignment or OPA algorithm proposed by Audsley [1] shall be subject of further reflection. Although OPA was originally proposed for non-suspending real-time systems with arbitrary deadlines, it can be applied for any schedulability test that is OPA-compatible, as defined below.
Definition 3 (OPA-Compatible [11]). A schedulability test that satisfies the following three conditions is termed OPAcompatible:
1) The schedulability of a task τ k may depend on the set of tasks with higher priority hp(τ k ), but not on their relative priority ordering.

2) The schedulability of a task τ k may depend on the set of tasks with lower priority lp(τ k ), but not on their relative priority ordering. 3) If the priorities of any two tasks of adjacent priority levels are swapped, the task being assigned to the higher priority level cannot become unschedulable if it was previously schedulable at the lower priority level.

In the course of OPA, the attempt is made to identify a task that can be assigned to the lowest priority level, under the assumption that all other tasks have higher priority, such that the system can be feasibly scheduled. This task is assigned to the lowest priority and removed from the set. Afterwards, this procedure is repeated for the remaining task set. The algorithm terminates if either all priority levels are mapped or no suitable task can be found for one particular priority level. The benefit of this priority assignment policy is the fact that, instead of examining all n! possible priority orderings, only O(n 2 ) priority orderings are taken into consideration. Proof. Each condition can be considered independently:

1) Since Theorem 2 and Theorem 3 do not depend on the relative order of hp(τ k ), the condition holds. 2) Similarly, Theorem 2 and Theorem 3 do not depend on lp(τ k ) at all. 3) When τ k is swapped with an adjacent task τ ∈ hp(τ k ), the accumulated maximum workload of hp(τ k ) that interferes with τ k decreases. Thus, τ k remains schedulable.

Owing to the fact that the schedulability test from Theorem 4 is OPA-compatible, we determine our task priorities by means of OPA adopting Theorem 4 as schedulability condition. This approach is referred to as SCAIR-OPA.
Theorem 5. If any priority assignments exist for which the condition in Theorem 4 holds, SCAIR-OPA returns one of these.
Proof. According to Lemma 4, the sufficient test Theorem 4 is compliant with the above conditions. Relating to the proof of Theorem 3 in [11], we conclude this theorem.

div.head: VI. EVALUATION
div.p: Having introduced our pseudo-polynomial time schedulability test SCAIR as summarized in Theorem 4, we will conduct comprehensive experiments in order to evaluate the proposed method. For this purpose, we generate synthetic task sets to which SCAIR as well as a selection of other algorithms are applied that are outlined below:

• XDM: A pseudo-polynomial time approach modeling suspension as computation for all tasks and applying TDA under a deadline-monotonic order. • SA-MILP: The MILP implemented by Biondi et al. [3] based on the errata in [26] of the original MILP in [25]. The priority assignment is deadline monotonic. To compare the above methods, we increase the system utilization successively within a range from 0% to 100% by steps of 1% and generate 100 task sets for each utilization level. In the course of this, we assess the results by means of the acceptance ratio, i.e., the number of task sets identified as schedulable divided by the total number of task sets on the particular utilization level. In our evaluation, we focus on the impact of three different task characteristics on the acceptance ratio, namely, the length and frequency of suspension intervals as well as the deviation between the upper and the lower bound of suspension times.

div.head: A. Experiment Setup
div.p: As a common basis for all experimental scenarios, we initially synthesize sets of 10 non-suspending sporadic tasks. In the course of this, the particular task utilization values for a given task set utilization level are generated by means of the UUniFast method [2], whereat the task periods are created according to a log-uniform distribution over the interval [1ms, 100ms] (for details regarding this approach refer to [12]), the worst-case execution time is specified as C i = T i •U i , and deadlines are implicit, i.e., D i = T i .

In a second step, we transform the previously created sporadic tasks into segmented self-suspending tasks. Since we aim to analyze the impact of a task's suspension length on the acceptance ratio in Sec. VI-B, we choose the total suspension length of each task according to a uniform random distribution, namely, in the range [0.01
div.formula: • (T i -C i ), 0.1 • (T i -C i )] if suspension intervals are short, in [0.1 • (T i -C i ), 0.6 • (T i -C i )] if suspension inter- vals are medium, and in [0.6 • (T i -C i ), (T i -C i )]
div.p: if suspension intervals are long. In Sec. VI-B, we assume that Ŝj i = Sj i for each suspension interval of each self-suspending task τ i .

However, in Sec. VI-C, we assign this generated value to Ŝj i and scale the lower-bound on the suspension time by a factor β ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}, i.e., Sj i = β • Ŝj i , since the impact of the suspension length lower-bound on the acceptance ratio is investigated at that point. Not least, the number of computation segments M i is chosen with respect to the actual suspension type, i.e., M i = 2 if suspension is rare, M i = 5 if suspension is moderate, and M i = 10 if suspension is frequent. Thereon, availing the obtained values, every single computation segment C j i as well as each suspension interval S j i is generated according to a uniform distribution. Henceforth, we proceed as follows: In Sec. VI-B as well as in Sec. VI-C, we first synthesize our test data as described above. Thereafter, we compare our method with the schedulability tests for dynamic self-suspending tasks listed above, employing a rate monotonic priority order as well as Audsley's Optimal Priority Assignment algorithm [1].

div.head: B. Performance under Varied Suspension Characteristics
div.p: Having conducted our experiments under the previously outlined settings, we illustrate the results in Fig. 8, which are discussed as follows: 1) comparison to all methods but SA-MILP, and 2) comparison to SA-MILP.

Evidently, XDM has a low acceptance rate and thus can only be applied sensibly when suspension intervals are short. While IdV-Burst-RM performs significantly better than XDM, it is still outperformed by PASS-OPA. These results, in turn, are overshot by SCAIR-OPA which clearly outperforms PASS-OPA in all scenarios. For reference only, we conducted experiments under SCAIR-RM as well, which achieves acceptance ratios close to PASS-OPA in most cases, but performs quite worse than SCAIR-OPA. According to Fig. 8a, d, g, the performance of SA-MILP highly depends on the suspension length. If suspension intervals are long, transforming a sporadic higher-priority task τ i comprising M i computation segments into M i sporadic tasks with jitters, as performed in SA-MILP, introduces a high level of pessimism. This follows from the fact that, due to the transformation, all M i computation segments of τ i may interfere with a lower-priority task τ k at the same time without taking their separation by suspension into account. To ensure that the evaluation of all task sets can be completed under SA-MILP, we specified a timeout of 5 minutes per task set. Such timeouts affect the smoothness of the acceptance ratio curves, especially observed in Fig. 8b as well as in Fig. 8c.
However, if the suspension length is short, our SCAIR-OPA approach is more pessimistic owing to its design as a more efficient and OPA-compatible schedulability test.

div.head: C. Performance under Varied Suspension Interval Bounds
div.p: Contemplating the most unfavorable out of the scenarios discussed in Sec. VI-B, i.e., long suspension intervals, we now drop the assumption that Ŝj i = Sj i ∀ S j i and evaluate the performance of SCAIR-OPA under different settings for Sj i as delineated in Sec. VI-A. From Fig. 9 it is obvious that, as observed earlier, the number of accepted task sets decreases with higher suspension frequency, while still surpassing PASS-OPA. Moreover, it is evident that an increasing gap between the upper and lower bounds on the suspension time, i.e., Ŝj i and Sj i , leads to a smaller number of schedulable task sets as well as to an earlier drop of the acceptance ratio. However, the discrepancy between the acceptance ratios of SCAIR-OPA-0 and SCAIR-OPA-100, i.e., β = 0 and β = 1, respectively, becomes smaller although not negligible when suspensions occur more frequently.

According to the above observations, the more the lower bound on the suspension time deviates from the upper bound, the less task sets can be deemed schedulable. Hence, it is worthwhile to specify lower bounds in such a way that they diverge only slightly from the upper bound, i.e., to avoid early completion of suspension intervals, in order to achieve higher acceptance ratios.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In this work, we derived the multi-segment workload function (cf. Def. 1) as well as, resulting from this, the maximum workload function (cf. Def. 2) which permits us to compute a safe upper bound on the workload a segmented self-suspending task contributes to a certain interval of time. We thereon proposed SCAIR (cf. Theorem 4), a safe schedulability test for segmented self-suspending task systems scheduled under a fixed-priority policy, and proved that it is OPA-compatible. We showed that the number of task sets schedulable by SCAIR-OPA can be enhanced by minimizing or even avoiding early completions of suspension intervals.
